Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection $\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]], [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters $x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give $m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so $m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure $m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures, and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them on the entire Borel sigma-algebra ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on $\mathbb T^n$ ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation (by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$. Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion, nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters proved below.

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$; 2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$; 3. consequently the Fourier expansion $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$ hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and 4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

derivations.claim: For each interval, choose an affine copy of the bump in [A1]. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. Its integral is finite and positive, so normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. Its derivative is $h$, and it vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$.

For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. Then $\int H=0$ by [A2]. Assuming the construction in dimension $d-1$, define
$$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$
Differentiating gives $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h-\theta_1H+\theta_1H=h$. The first component vanishes both before the support and after its total first-coordinate integral, which is zero; the other components are compactly supported by induction.

If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the support of $\theta_i$; for the first component also include the interval hull of these supports. The recursive formulas then place every output component inside the fixed compact product $K'=\prod_iJ_i$. Every output derivative is a finite sum of fixed-bump derivatives times finite-coordinate integrals of derivatives of $h$ or its marginals. Such integrals have sup norm at most the interval length times the integrand sup norm, and differentiation in other coordinates commutes with integration. Induction therefore bounds each output seminorm by a constant times finitely many input seminorms. This proves fixed-support continuity.

when $\sigma>j+d/2$.

The derivative Fourier series through order $j$ are absolutely and uniformly convergent by step 1.1. Their partial sums are derivatives of finite Fourier sums; the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus in each coordinate identifies the uniform limits successively as the classical derivatives of the limit. For polynomials, $\widehat{fg}(k)=\sum_\ell\widehat f(k-\ell)\widehat g(\ell)$. Discrete Young, obtained by Minkowski's inequality on finite translates, yields
$\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\le C(\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|\widehat g\|_{\ell^1}+\|\widehat f\|_{\ell^1}\|g\|_{H^\sigma})\le C\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma}$,
since step 1.1 with $j=0$ bounds both coefficient $\ell^1$ norms.

Finite Fourier sums are dense by the completion in [F1], so the polynomial product estimate extends uniquely by Cauchy convergence to $H^\sigma$. Since step 1.1 also gives convergence in $C^0$, this extended product agrees pointwise with multiplication of the continuous representatives. For a trigonometric polynomial approximation, the $k$th coefficient of the commutator is
$\sum_{v+\ell=k}(w_k^m-w_\ell^m)\widehat f(v)i\ell_j\widehat g(\ell)$.

$|w_{\ell+v}^m-w_\ell^m|\le C_m|v|(w_v^{m-1}+w_\ell^{m-1})$,
